title: States of Matter and the Kinetic Molecular Theory

standard_code: SSS 1 Chemistry: States of Matter and the Kinetic Molecular Theory
standard_text: The three states of matter; melting point, boiling point and heating and cooling curves; the kinetic molecular theory: matter is made of particles in constant motion with forces between them. (summary of the senior secondary Chemistry curriculum, SSS 1; WAEC and NECO syllabuses)
meta_desc: Free SSS 1 Chemistry worksheets (senior secondary curriculum, WAEC and NECO): the kinetic molecular theory, particles in solids, liquids and gases, temperature and internal energy, heating and cooling curves and melting points and boiling points. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles.
body_html:
How to think about it

In a solid, particles vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid they move past each other; in a gas they move freely and far apart. Heating gives the particles more kinetic energy.

On a heating curve the temperature stays constant while a substance melts or boils: the energy is used to overcome the forces between the particles. The melting point and boiling point can identify a pure substance.

Example

Why does the temperature stay the same while ice melts?

Energy breaks the forces between molecules.

Answer: the energy is used to overcome intermolecular forces, not to raise the kinetic energy

Example

In which state are the forces between particles weakest?

Particles are far apart.

Answer: gas

Common mistakes

  • Thinking particles stop moving in a solid.
  • Thinking temperature rises while water boils.
  • Mixing up evaporation and boiling.

faq.q: What is the difference between boiling and evaporation?
faq.a: Evaporation happens at the surface at any temperature; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

faq.q: Why does a gas fill its container?
faq.a: Its particles move quickly in all directions and the forces between them are very weak.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “Particles only vibrate about fixed positions.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Some air is let out of a basketball (volume and temperature stay the same). What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: Fewer particles hit the walls each second.

items.q: Why does a metal rod expand when it is heated?
c: The particles vibrate more and move slightly further apart.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: A sealed can of gas is heated. What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: The particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and with more force.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “It has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: A sealed balloon of air is left in the hot sun. What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: The particles gain kinetic energy and hit the walls harder and more often, and the balloon expands.

items.q: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of oxygen molecules (molar mass 0.0320 kg/mol) at 500 K.
items.e: ½m crms² = (3/2)kT, crms = √(3kT/m) = 624 m/s.

items.q: Why can a liquid flow?
c: Its particles can slide past one another.

items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: What happens to the particles of a gas when its temperature rises?

items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: A sealed can of gas is heated. Why does the pressure increase?
c: The particles hit each other more often, not the walls.

items.e: Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls of the container.

sets.title: Particles in solids, liquids and gases

items.q: How do the particles move in a liquid?
items.e: In a liquid the particles are closely packed in a random arrangement, sliding past one another, with strong forces of attraction, but weaker than in a solid.

items.q: Why is a gas easy to compress?
c: There are large spaces between its particles.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: When are two objects in thermal equilibrium?
c: when they are at the same temperature, so there is no net heat flow
when they have the same mass
when they have the same internal energy
items.e: This is the basis of the zeroth law.

items.q: A gas absorbs 700 J of heat and does 350 J of work on its surroundings. What is the change in its internal energy?
items.e: First law: ΔU = Q − W = 350 J.

items.q: What is the first law of thermodynamics?
c: heat always flows from cold to hot
the change in internal energy equals heat added minus work done by the system (ΔU = Q − W)
energy is lost in every change
temperature can never reach absolute zero
items.e: It is conservation of energy.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, bromine (Br<sub>2</sub>) or ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>)?
